extracted.intended_audience: researchers, scientists, and other readers interested in post-publication peer review and using PubPeer
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical information for commenting on published scientific papers via PubPeer, including privacy options, moderation rules, what to comment on, and how to search and create accounts. Targeted at people who want to perform or learn about post-publication peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication peer review: scope of reviewer critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers can comment on weaknesses of the manuscript, such as flawed methods, far-fetched conclusions, missing references, or missed hypotheses, and suggest improvements. After their evaluation, the peer reviewers will determine if the manuscript could be accepted for publication if the suggested edits are included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the traditional role of pre-publication peer review as improving manuscripts and acting as the 'golden standard' for evaluating and improving quality before publication. Use pre-publication review to identify methodological flaws, unjustified conclusions, and missing literature or hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review is valid
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper can also be commented on after publication; scientific knowledge keeps on growing, and scientists should be allowed to comment on papers even after they have been published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames PPPR as complementary to pre-publication review — useful because new information or concerns can emerge after publication; encourages using platforms like PubPeer to surface shortcomings that may prompt corrections or retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stick to facts and public verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements need to stick to facts and be publicly verifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example guidance: one could say that two images look very similar to each other, but not say that the authors committed fraud. This rule is enforced by moderation; comments that violate it (especially from new accounts) may be removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unproven accusations (no declaring fraud)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assert that authors committed fraud; restrict claims to observable, verifiable issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use objective descriptions of the evidence (e.g., image similarity, duplication) rather than attributing intent. This reduces defamatory or unconstructive commentary and aligns with PubPeer moderation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civility and constructiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to keep the discussions constructive and civil, PubPeer has several guidelines for posting comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should remain civil and polite — similar expectations as (anonymous) pre-publication peer review. Civil tone helps maintain usefulness and uptake; uncivil comments risk removal and harm the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of new accounts and removals for rule violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments from new accounts are moderated and occasionally removed if they violate rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New accounts are subject to scrutiny; moderation enforces factual/verifiable statements and civility. Expect that allegations or non-evidence-based posts from new or unregistered accounts may be taken down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity options and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: PubPeer allows users to choose between leaving signed comments (under their real name) or anonymous — which quickly became the most popular choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: anonymity allows people to reveal scientific misconduct without repercussions for their career (similar rationale to anonymous pre-publication peer review). Disadvantages: critics argue anonymity could enable hateful or false comments, though the author argues most scientists remain objective and polite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical recommendation on using anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: I would recommend to not start posting under your full name, unless you are confident that your comment would not harm your career, or if you have something positive to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For newcomers, prefer anonymous/unregistered posting for critical comments; use full name for positive or low-risk commentary. Store secret keys safely if using anonymous registered accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account and privacy mechanics (registered anonymous & unregistered)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymous accounts get a name from the tree of life and 'a secret key' — a 16 digit password. In 2013 PubPeer introduced anonymous without registration ('unregistered'), and in 2016 PubPeer stopped keeping track of IP addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registered anonymous accounts allow logging in with a secret key and switching between identity modes; unregistered comments are possible and are shown as 'unregistered'. PubPeer's no-IP-logging policy increases commenter privacy and legal protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple accounts permitted and switching identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters can thus create multiple accounts, and switch between them, or switch between anonymous and full-name comment mode easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because usernames are non-identifying and keyed by secret keys, users may maintain multiple personas for different commenting needs; be mindful of site guidelines and moderation regardless of account multiplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of valid substantive critiques to raise
rubrics_metrics.description: Most 'unreg' comments revealed serious concerns about papers, such as image duplication and manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Image problems are common and legitimate grounds for public comment; raising such observable issues has led to many corrections and retractions (e.g., Obokata STAP case). Use concrete examples and evidence when pointing out such problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search and discovery practices on PubPeer
rubrics_metrics.description: You can type in the name of the DOI, PMID or author to search for papers. You can also search for particular commenters by typing in: Users: <name>.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes: the 'Users:' search can be picky and may require being logged in; example working searches include 'users: bik' or 'users: "Elisabeth M Bik"'. Use DOIs/PMIDs for precise paper lookup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use browser extensions to get alerts
rubrics_metrics.description: There are very helpful PubPeer extensions for your favorite browser (Chrome, Firefox) that alert you for comments on papers, for example during PubMed searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensions are not perfect but helpful; they can surface comments while browsing literature and increase awareness of flagged concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive comments welcomed
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive comments are always appreciated, of course!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have praise or confirmatory observations, consider signing or using full-name mode if appropriate; positive feedback contributes to a balanced post-publication record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect impact: PPPR can lead to corrections/retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: PubPeer has become a very useful tool for the public posting of shortcomings or concerns in scientific papers. It has led to many corrections and retractions of problematic papers that otherwise would not have been noticed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By documenting verifiable problems publicly, PPPR can increase the chance of correction or retraction; historical examples (Obokata STAP, users with many flagged papers) illustrate the potential consequences of well-documented public critiques.
